newsitem.title: UK: British Conservative income tax plans questioned.
newsitem.headline: British Conservative income tax plans questioned.

text.p: Britain's Conservative Party wants the income tax rate to drop to 20 percent from 23 percent but economists say this would require public spending to be cut to the bone or taxes to be raised elsewhere.

Prime Minister John Major, launching his ruling party's election manifesto on Wednesday, said a standard 20 percent income tax rate remained an aspiration. The Conservatives are tax-cutters by instinct, he said.
The other main plank of Conservative fiscal policy is to virtually eliminate public borrowing by the turn of the century.

But at the same time, the manifesto pledges to spend more on hospitals, schools and the police. Public sector debt is forecast at 26.4 billion pounds ($43.5 billion) this year, falling to 19.2 billion next.

"To make ends meet, we need increases in taxes, a great deal of restraint in public spending and rapid economic growth," said Martin Weale, director of the National Institute for Economic and Social Research and one of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's independent advisers.
Elections are set for May 1 and the Conservatives lag in the opinion polls, although the latest one shows the wide gap may be closing.
Weale said the next government, of whichever colour, could move to a 20 pence basic income tax rate by raising other taxes. He suggested corporation tax and tax relief on mortgage interest payments.
Conservative ministers have also been evasive when asked if value added tax (VAT) would be extended in future.
Clarke told BBC radio that the overall amount of tax paid, as a proportion of national income, had stayed about the same since 1992, despite a one penny cut in standard income tax to 23 percent.

The opposition Labour Party accuses the government of 22 tax rises since 1992 but most people would be hard-pushed to list them. Cutting headline tax rates and clawing back revenue from elsewhere is nothing new.
But Britain's public services -- particularly health and social security -- will again feel the squeeze of both Conservative and Labour ambitions to lower tax.

"Inevitably, if they have long-term aspirations to reduce the basic rate to 20p, the pressure is really going to come on the public services," said Alissa Goodman, research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies.
Spending plans are already extremely tight, she said, and the Labour Party has promised it would stick to the government's plans for the next two years.
The Conservative manifesto said National Health Service spending would rise each year as economic growth continued. But, as Weale noted, assuming years of unbroken growth is some leap of faith.
The manifesto also said the Private Finance Initiative -- a scheme to encourage private firms to invest in infrastructure projects -- would unleash a new flow of funds into the NHS.
But the PFI has been slow to take off and, according to Goodman, the real level of public infrastructure investment would fall dramatically even if it came in according to plan.
"The PFI is not a cost-cutting plan anyway," Weale said. "We know that when the private sector borrows, its cost of borrowing is higher than the government's."

One long-term Conservative plan that could reduce public debt is a "Basic Pensions Plus" scheme. That would effectively privatise the state pension by paying a proportion of a person's national insurance payments into a pooled fund, run by the private sector, to invest on their behalf.
But the scheme will be phased in over 40 years. "It will be be of some help but that's a long, long way away," Weale said.
One Conservative tax break announced on Wednesday would allow some non-working married people to transfer tax allowances to a working spouse -- netting them about 17.50 pounds a week.

The Labour Party said it would cost 3.2 to five billion pounds but economists thought less. "Even if it is 2.0 billion they have 200 tax allowances they could play with so they could raise revenue elsewhere," HSBC economist Dharshini David said.
Nonetheless, the Conservatives have not said how this tax break would be funded.

"Both parties face the same arithmetic and the Labour Party might face more pressure to spend," Weale said. Old allies, the public sector unions, will push hard to end years of pay restraint if Labour takes power. ($ = 0.606 British Pounds)
